02_six_moves: Most people train for years and still look the same.
You know why? Because they're doing the wrong exercises.
Today I'll give you six moves that build more muscle than anything you've done before.
No barbell. No gym.
And here's what sounds impossible:
science explains why they beat your favorite gym exercises.
But first: which of these six do studies rate as better for triceps than the close-grip bench press?
You'll find out soon. Stay with me.
Think about what happens when you squat with a barbell.
Hundreds of pounds pressing straight down on your spine.
Rep after rep, year after year.
Heavy doesn't mean effective.
Same with the bench press.
Most people who've trained for over ten years carry the damage in their joints.
Here's what science actually says about muscle growth.
The main driver of growth isn't the weight on the bar.
It's muscle tension.
Number one: pull-ups.
Most people think pull-ups are just a back exercise. They're wrong.
Do them right, and your lats, upper back, rear delts, biceps, forearms and core
all work at max to lift your whole body through space.
A lat pulldown machine will never give you that.
The machine dictates the path. Your stabilizers switch off.
In pull-ups, every muscle works full out.
Grip slightly wider than shoulders, arms fully straight.
Pull your chest to the bar, not your chin.
Pause at the top. Lower slowly, five seconds down. No momentum.
Can't do a single one? Start with dead hangs and slow negatives.
Jump to the top and fight gravity on the way down.
Hit ten clean reps? Put on a weighted vest.
That's where real size comes from.
Number two: inverted rows.
There's a pulling pattern most programs almost completely ignore.
And that's exactly why so many people have rounded shoulders and chronic pain.
Inverted rows hit your mid back, traps, rear delts and rhomboids through a full range
with zero load on your spine.
Find something at waist height: a sturdy table, TRX straps, parallel bars.
Grip slightly wider than shoulders, body in a straight line from head to heels.
Pull your chest to the bar. At the top, squeeze your shoulder blades hard.
Lower with control.
Raise the bar: easier. Lower it: harder. Feet on a box: advanced.
Three sets of eight to twelve, with a one second hold at the top.
Number three: dips.
Remember the exercise that beats the close-grip bench for triceps?
This is it.
And here's the one thing that separates safe dips from dangerous ones:
shoulder blades down and back the entire time. Keep them locked.
Lean forward a little to shift the focus to your chest.
Lower until your shoulders are parallel to the floor. One second pause at the bottom.
Press up. Explosive.
Not ready for dips? Start with bench dips.
Hands on the edge of a bench. Ninety degree angle. Press up.
Hit fifteen to twenty clean reps? Move to the bars.
Hit twelve to fifteen on the bars? Add weight.
Chest, shoulder and triceps mass from weighted dips is some of the most functional you can build.
Number four: decline push-ups.
Standard push-ups are a good move, but once you can do twenty clean reps, they stop building muscle.
Most people answer with more reps, and wonder why their chest won't grow.
The problem isn't volume. It's range of motion and load angle.
With your feet elevated, you do two things at once.
One: you shift the load to your upper chest and front delts.
Two: you increase how much bodyweight your muscles move every rep.
But here's the detail that explains the extra growth.
Studies on training muscles in a stretched position keep showing superior growth.
In some, fifty to one hundred percent more.
Feet on a box, eighteen to twenty-four inches high.
Hands on the floor, slightly wider than shoulders. Body completely rigid.
No sagging hips.
Lower your chest slowly, three to four seconds.
Press up with control. Three sets of eight to twelve.
Hit fifteen clean? Raise your feet higher or put on a vest.
Number five: Bulgarian split squats.
You've been waiting for a leg exercise. Here it is.
And if you've never done these seriously, get ready
for everything you know about leg training to fall apart.
Bulgarian split squats build more quad and glute muscle than barbell squats,
with zero load on your spine.
Stand two steps in front of a bench. Rear foot on it, laces down.
Slowly lower your back knee to the floor.
Feel the deep stretch in the back hip, and a serious burn in the front quad.
Three sets of eight to ten per leg.
Master this, and you'll build legs that work on a whole other level.
Number six: single-leg Romanian deadlift.
Hinge on one leg, flat back, feel your hamstrings stretch, then drive back up.
Six exercises. Pull-ups and inverted rows for a back that's actually thick and functional.
Decline push-ups and dips for chest, shoulders and triceps that beat most pressing programs.
Bulgarian split squats and single-leg deadlifts for legs that carry over to everything you do.
Train this two to three times a week.
Keep adding reps or resistance.
Don't chase load before you own the movement. Movement is the mechanism.
Do this for six months, and you'll build more real muscle than most people do in years at the gym,
while keeping the joints that make it all possible.
03_saitama_workout: One hundred push-ups. One hundred sit-ups. One hundred squats. And a ten kilometer run.
Every single day.
This is the most famous workout in anime.
The hero who did it says it made him the strongest man alive, and cost him every hair on his head.
So what happens if a normal person actually does it?
And here's the question: one part of this program is almost useless. Can you guess which one?
Stick around. The answer might surprise you.
The rules are simple. Four exercises.
No weights. No gym. No days off.
Thirty days in a row.
Day one. Push-ups.
The first twenty feel easy.
By thirty, the form breaks down. Hips sag, elbows flare, and every rep gets uglier.
The fix: split it up. Ten sets of ten, with short breaks. Same hundred reps, clean form.
Then come one hundred squats, and the legs start burning around rep sixty.
Then the sit-ups. Then the run.
Next morning, everything hurts.
That soreness is muscle damage from a load your body has never seen.
In the first week you actually feel weaker, not stronger. Your body is still repairing.
By week two, something changes.
The push-ups get clean. The squats stop burning.
Your heart, lungs and muscles adapt to the volume fast.
Ten kilometers a day is around seventy kilometers a week. That burns a lot of fat.
And now, the answer. The almost useless part? The sit-ups.
Your abs are already there. They're just hidden under a layer of fat.
A hundred sit-ups won't burn the belly fat on top of them. The running and your diet will.
And here's the real problem with the whole program.
After two weeks, a hundred reps is no longer a challenge. It's endurance work.
Muscles grow from progressive overload. When the work never gets harder, the growth stops.
Day thirty.
Body fat is down, mostly thanks to the running.
Endurance went through the roof.
Muscle? A little more. But nowhere near a superhero.
And the hair? Still there. No study links push-ups to hair loss.
So here's how to make this workout actually work.
One: swap plain push-ups for harder versions. Feet on a box, slower reps, fewer but tougher sets.
Two: replace sit-ups with planks and leg raises. They train the whole core, not just the top of your abs.
Three: take one or two rest days a week, and sleep. Muscles grow when you recover, not when you train.
And ten kilometers every day? Thirty to forty minutes of cardio is plenty.
You won't become the strongest hero in thirty days.
But you'll be stronger than you were yesterday. And that's the version that counts.
Write day one in the comments, and start tomorrow.
04_walking_belly_fat: This cookie has six hundred calories.
To burn it off, you'd have to sprint for fifty-five minutes.
Fifty-five minutes of sweat, gasping and pain. For one snack.
You can't outrun your fork.
But you can outsmart your metabolism.
Most people think fitness is a pain contest.
They sprint, do HIIT, suffer, and look exactly the same six months later.
Today I'll show you a walking protocol that doesn't just burn calories. It hacks your insulin.
Give me six minutes, and I'll save you ten years of useless cardio.
You diet for weeks. Your face gets leaner. Your arms get leaner.
But the belt around your waist doesn't move.
That's not laziness. It's a defense system.
Back in the nineties, researchers found that fat cells have switches.
Beta receptors are a green light. Adrenaline hits them, the cell opens, and the energy burns.
Your face, arms and chest are full of them. That's why they lean out first.
Alpha receptors are a red light. The cell locks its doors and holds on to the fat.
And belly fat has far more of these red lights than the rest of your body.
Evolution put them there to protect your organs from starvation.
Here's the trap. Sprints, CrossFit, brutal intervals.
They flood your body with stress hormones: adrenaline and cortisol.
In your arms, adrenaline hits the green light. In your belly, it hits the red one.
And chronically high cortisol is directly linked to belly fat storage.
You're literally working harder to stay fatter.
Picture two fuel tanks.
Tank A is small and high octane. That's sugar, for sprinting and heavy lifting.
Tank B is a giant tanker. That's your body fat, for slow, long, easy work.
A big review of fifty-four studies found the same thing.
High intensity burns mostly sugar. Low intensity burns mostly fat.
When you run, you burn your lunch. When you walk, you burn your belly.
While walking you can still talk. That's zone two. Cortisol stays low, and the red lights stay quiet.
So the answer is walking.
But strolling around the couch won't give you abs. Or every mailman would be shredded.
On paper, running wins: about three fifty calories in thirty minutes, versus one fifty for walking.
But you're not a spreadsheet. Hard training spikes ghrelin, your hunger hormone.
An hour later you're starving. Extra bread with butter: four hundred calories.
Congratulations. You suffered thirty minutes to end up plus fifty.
And you're wiped out. Couch, elevator, less moving all day.
Walking doesn't spike your hunger and doesn't drain you.
One hour a day is three hundred calories. That's twenty-one hundred a week, and about fourteen kilos of fat a year.
The runner quits in three weeks with sore knees. The walker wins, because he never stops.
Here's the protocol. Insulin is a storage hormone. While it's high, fat burning is switched off.
Step one: the after-meal walk.
Research shows a ten minute walk right after eating controls blood sugar far better than walking at any other time.
Your rule: three ten minute walks a day. After breakfast, after lunch, after dinner.
That's thirty minutes of cardio and three thousand steps, without changing into gym clothes.
Your muscles burn the meal as fuel instead of storing it on your belly.
Step two: NEAT. The calories you burn just by living. It can differ by two thousand a day between lean and heavy people.
Hack one: park at the far end. Plus four hundred steps.
Hack two: never sit on a phone call. Walk around.
Hack three: kill the elevator. Stairs burn three times more.
Do all that and you'll hit eight to ten thousand steps almost by accident.
Step three, for the impatient: incline walking. The nuclear option.
It doubles the workload without the impact of running. Your glutes and hamstrings work at maximum.
The viral twelve three thirty: incline twelve, speed three, thirty minutes.
One rule: don't hold the rails. Grab them, and incline twelve becomes incline two.
Can't do it hands free? Drop to eight. Two or three sessions a week.
But if you eat like a trash can, none of this works.
Remember the cookie: an hour of walking to burn it, forty-five seconds to eat it.
Food is the engine. Walking is the turbo. No fuel in the tank, and the car goes nowhere.
A small daily deficit, plus this protocol, and the fat has nowhere left to hide.
Weeks one to four: check your average steps, add two thousand, and walk after every meal.
Weeks five to eight: at least eight thousand steps a day. Rain or snow. Add the hacks.
Weeks nine to twelve: ten to twelve thousand steps, plus two incline sessions.
Walking is the oldest movement we have. It clears your head, saves your joints, and burns belly fat.
My challenge: seven days. Track your steps, and walk ten minutes after every meal.
Come back in a week. More energy, less bloating, and looser pants.
01_50_squats_en: What happens if you do FIFTY squats every day?
No barbell. No gym. Just YOU and your body.
Watch till the end, most people quit RIGHT before the best part.
Squats are one of the most POWERFUL bodyweight exercises.
They work your legs, glutes, core, and even your lower back.
And the best part? You can do them ANYWHERE. Anytime.
Week one.
Your legs and glutes are gonna BURN.
That's normal, your muscles are rebuilding and getting STRONGER.
Week two.
Your legs feel steadier, your moves more confident, and climbing stairs gets WAY easier.
Week three.
Balance, coordination, and endurance hit a whole NEW level.
After a month, fifty squats will feel like a WARM-UP.
Stronger legs, better posture, thanks to a solid core.
But let's be honest... this won't make you a BODYBUILDER.
Want size? Add weight: dumbbells, a barbell, or resistance bands.
But as a foundation, it's TOP tier.
Mobility, flexibility, circulation, strong knees and ankles.
And the BIGGEST bonus: confidence.
When your body moves, you control not just your muscles... but your WHOLE life.
So is it worth starting? ABSOLUTELY.
Fifty too many? Split it into sets.
Already strong? Try seventy-five or a hundred. The key is EVERY day.
Subscribe, only honest advice here. And tell me in the comments how many squats YOU do.
Small steps every day. BIG changes.
